eligibility_note: Own CS-ARDL estimation; exposure is AI (VC investment in AI); 8 economies meets the 3-economy AI threshold; outcome is HDI (living standards beyond income). Eligible, though the AI measure is internally inconsistent (see problems).

income_group_note: No income-group analysis in the paper; record's 'not reported' / 'not applicable' entries are correct (sample is 7 high-income economies plus China and India by external classification, which the paper does not state).

risk_of_bias.confounding_reverse_causation: agree (serious): N=8, T=12 CS-ARDL with no instrument; the paper's own literature review cites evidence of causality running from growth to AI, and the paper never addresses it, yet it uses 'effect/impact' language.
risk_of_bias.exposure_measurement: agree (serious): VC investment in AI in USD millions (not scaled) is a funding flow, and the methodology section says robot installations are the AI indicator, contradicting Table I.
risk_of_bias.selection_of_countries_years: agree (serious): eight hand-picked leading robot markets, T=12, and the conclusion mislabels the sample as G7 although it includes China, India and South Korea.
risk_of_bias.outcome_measurement: agree (moderate): HDI is a slow-moving composite that includes an income component while GDP per capita is a regressor; Table I lists World Bank as the source.
risk_of_bias.specification: agree (serious): three alternative models each omit one control, lag order and CSA terms not reported, Model 3 SEs and t-stats of 50-62 are implausible, and equations say log(PCI), log(INF), log(FDI) while Table V PCI coefficients (6.16E-05) look like level terms and inflation/FDI can be negative.
risk_of_bias.selective_reporting: too_harsh (moderate would fit): all three models are shown, the insignificant Model 2 is disclosed in the text, and the conclusion cites only Models 1 and 3 as significant; the real omission is that the abstract promises short-run results that are never reported, and the abstract claim of a 'substantial effect' overstates 2 of 3 models.
risk_of_bias.why: Causal language, an AI measure that conflicts with its own description, a tiny hand-picked sample and fragile, inconsistent specifications justify serious overall.

problems: Internal inconsistencies in the paper rather than in the record: (a) methodology says robot installations are the AI indicator but Table I says VC investment in AI (OECD); (b) conclusion says 'G7 countries' but lists China, India, South Korea; (c) Table IV caption repeats 'Cross-sectional Dependency Test' and its star legend is reversed ('*, ** and *** represent 1%, %5 and 10%'); (d) abstract says short-run relationships analysed but only long-run is in Table V; (e) in Equation 2 and 3 the PCI/INF terms are inconsistently included (Model 3 has no PCI). Record is otherwise accurate; no invented content found.

eligibility_note: Borderline but acceptable: ICT-capital contributions are taken from Timmer et al. (2003), but the author performs own kernel-density, Li bootstrap and Silverman tests on 15 developed economies; outcome is labour productivity. No regression estimate of an ICT effect.

sample_corrections.n_economies: 15 (US plus 14 EU countries; Table 1 also prints an 'European Union' aggregate row that is not a country). Printed unweighted averages recompute to the 14 non-US rows (non-ICT about 0.79, TFP about 1.07, GDP per hour about 2.18), not the 15-country mean, so the record's description of the average as a 15-country mean is not supported by the table.

income_group_note: All 15 economies are developed; no income-group estimates exist. Record's entries are correct.

risk_of_bias.confounding_reverse_causation: agree (serious): growth-accounting contributions are not causal estimates, the TFP residual absorbs ICT spillovers (author concedes), and the text uses 'caused'/'driving force' language with no strategy for reverse causation.
risk_of_bias.exposure_measurement: agree (moderate): ICT capital contribution is a sound exposure concept but is borrowed from a secondary source with no construction details here.
risk_of_bias.selection_of_countries_years: too_harsh (moderate would fit): the 15 countries are described as almost the whole population of developed economies and chosen by ICT-capital data availability; the short 1980-1995 window mainly limits relevance to the later ICT boom.
risk_of_bias.outcome_measurement: agree (moderate): GDP per hour levels are reconstructed from contribution tables by the author's own base-year procedure.
risk_of_bias.specification: agree (serious): n=15 gives low power (the author says so), a rule-of-thumb bandwidth is used 'for the sake of time' for the Li bootstrap, and conclusions on TFP lean on a Silverman result while the Li-test on the same counterfactual is insignificant.
risk_of_bias.selective_reporting: agree (moderate): all seven Li p-values are shown, but interpretation emphasises the one significant Silverman result.
risk_of_bias.why: Causal wording on an accounting decomposition with tiny n and low-power tests; informative as descriptive evidence but not as an estimate of ICT impact.

problems: No invented content. Minor points: the Table 1 'unweighted average' row does not recompute as a 15-country mean (see sample_corrections); the 'European Union' row in Table 1 is an aggregate; the text sentence about Li-test power at p=0.2480 is garbled and contradicts the surrounding 'not significant' reading; footnote 5 on the rule-of-thumb bandwidth is on p.29 as the record says.

eligibility_note: Borderline on exposure: the AI measure is industrial robot stock per million employees, and the author states findings are about industrial automation rather than AI broadly (AI-patent stock only in a robustness row). Kept because it is framed and tested as AI; 64 economies, own FE/GMM estimation, outcome energy poverty (living standards/resource cost). Reviewer may wish to flag as robot-proxy.

sample_corrections.income_groups_covered: Paper states high (28), upper-middle (24), lower-middle (12), no low-income. However, by usual World Bank classification the Appendix A list appears to contain well over 28 high-income economies (e.g. about 38 by my count of Belgium, Canada, Chile, ..., US); the 28/24/12 split cannot be reconciled from the printed list, so treat the income counts as unverified.

heterogeneity.correction: No formal income-group split; income groups appear only in Fig. 4(b); the abstract and Section 5.4 restrict applicability. Appendix note gives 28/24/12 (but see sample note about the list not reconciling).

income_group_note: No income-group-specific estimates; record's 'not reported separately' is correct. Income-group counts in the Appendix A note do not obviously match the printed country list.

risk_of_bias.confounding_reverse_causation: agree (moderate): authors explicitly claim only conditional associations and use Sys-GMM, 2SLS and Bartik IV, but exclusion restrictions are argued verbally, no first-stage numbers are printed, instrumenting of the quadratic term is unclear, and robot stock tracks income (r=0.71 with GDP per capita).
risk_of_bias.exposure_measurement: agree (serious): industrial robot stock per million employees is manufacturing automation, which the authors concede is not AI broadly; patent stock is only a robustness row.
risk_of_bias.selection_of_countries_years: agree (moderate): balanced panel of 64 chosen by IFR and energy-poverty data availability, no low-income economies, 20-year window.
risk_of_bias.outcome_measurement: agree (moderate): geometric-mean composite whose per-capita electricity and energy components rise with development, so the index partly reflects income; electricity-access-only check is reported only in summary form.
risk_of_bias.specification: agree (moderate): quadratic form chosen a priori with many specifications; Table 7 anomalies (main-effect coefficients 0.082-0.121 vs 0.0517 at baseline despite mean-centred Z; text marginal effects of -0.010, +0.008, -0.028 do not recompute from Column 2, which gives about +0.006 at mean HC, +0.005 and +0.008); 'three-way interaction' mislabels two-way interactions; no GMM instrument count.
risk_of_bias.selective_reporting: agree (moderate): every robustness check and both channels support the hypotheses, full tables are only in an Online Appendix, interactions are significant at 10% only, and table notes retain revision language ('previously 5.21', 'formerly Table 3', coefficients 'now reported to four decimal places' to make turning points consistent), which weakens confidence in reported figures.
risk_of_bias.why: The robot proxy does not measure AI as the paper frames it, which by the guide justifies serious overall even though the paper correctly avoids causal claims.

problems: Record is accurate on all checked numbers. Additional issues in the paper: Table 7 text marginal effects do not reproduce from the table (record already notes this); Table 10 note says the inverted-U is confirmed at 5% for all rows although several coefficients are only significant at 10% and no Lind-Mehlum statistics are shown; the introduction describes the index as three components while Table 4 lists four; Appendix A says fewer than 10 SSA countries but the list has only South Africa; and the income-group counts (28/24/12) look inconsistent with the printed list. The record's statement 'all eight reported checks' should read seven alternative specifications plus baseline.

risk_of_bias.confounding_reverse_causation: agree (serious): PMG/ARDL without instruments or timing design, text claims it handles endogeneity, conclusion concedes results are correlational.
risk_of_bias.exposure_measurement: agree (serious): the PCA ICT index is internally inconsistent (Table 3 skew/kurtosis and Table 4 correlation 1.000 equal MCS; Tables 6-7 statistics equal IUI; Table 2 loadings differ from either), so what it measures is unclear.
risk_of_bias.selection_of_countries_years: agree (moderate): 26 SSA countries by data availability, balanced 1992-2023 (N=832 equals 26 x 32); Section 3.3 states 1991 to 2022; country list not shown.
risk_of_bias.outcome_measurement: agree (moderate): dependent variables are sector value-added shares of GDP (Table 3 means 21.3, 26.1, 45.9), described as 'growth'; Table 3 also shows agriculture minimum -2.51 and industry minimum 0.0000, which cannot be log-transformed as LnAGRV/LnINDV in Tables 6-7.
risk_of_bias.specification: agree (serious): four ICT measures entered one at a time with interactions, inconsistent log/level treatment, table numbering in text does not match, and in Tables 9-11 the control-variable coefficients and SEs in columns 2 and 4 are identical even though the ICT regressors differ.
risk_of_bias.selective_reporting: agree (serious, arguably critical): Table 10 and Table 11 columns 2-4 are identical in all long-run and short-run rows and the constant, despite different dependent variables (e.g. LNTO -0.0396*, -0.1151***, -0.0978***; ICT_INF 0.2594), and the text reports 0.26 for both sectors.
risk_of_bias.why: Duplicated coefficient blocks across the industry and services tables, plus an ICT index whose identity is unclear, mean the headline industry and services conclusions cannot be relied on; this is closer to critical than serious.

problems: Record is accurate on printed values. Issues beyond the record: (a) Table 10/11 columns 2-4 duplication and the identical control blocks in columns 2 and 4 of Tables 9-11 indicate copy-paste or generation errors, so sector attribution of printed results is unreliable; (b) text says all four interactions are negative and significant but TO_FTS is not; (c) text says 0.13-0.18 for agriculture LNTO while the table range is 0.09-0.18; (d) record locators: the 'largely insignificant' sentence is on p.115 and the ICT_INF 0.26 text is on p.115 (industry) and p.116 (services), not p.114 and p.116/117; (e) mixed I(0)/I(1) variables are not by themselves a problem for PMG/ARDL, so the record's point is weaker than stated, but I(0) dependent variables with ln of non-positive minima (Table 3) are.
